item.title: 💗 What's the difference between “required” and “preferred” skills in a job descr
item.description:
💗 What's the difference between “required” and “preferred” skills in a job description? 👀

» Required skills are the qualifications a company considers essential for the position.

» Preferred skills are additional qualifications that could strengthen your application, but aren't necessarily mandatory.

So if you meet the core requirements but you're missing a few preferred skills, the role may still be worth applying for.

The key is understanding which qualifications are essential and which are simply nice to have.

item.title: 💗 Quick reminder for Web3 job seekers! 👀 You don't need to meet every single req
item.description:
💗 Quick reminder for Web3 job seekers! 👀

You don't need to meet every single requirement in a job description to consider applying.

Some requirements are essential, while others describe the company's ideal candidate.

Focus on whether you can handle the core responsibilities, meet the mandatory requirements and demonstrate relevant experience.

Don't reject yourself from an opportunity before the hiring team has even reviewed your application!

item.description:
🔈 The Work Behind a Crypto Exchange

Ever wondered what actually happens after you place a trade on a centralized crypto exchange?

The process involves much more than matching buyers and sellers.

Trading systems process orders, internal records track balances, financial operations investigate discrepancie and risk and support teams help handle unexpected issues.

Our latest article explains how these processes work together and the different professional responsibilities involved.

It's a useful look at why crypto exchanges need people working across engineering, finance, operations, security, compliance and customer support.

item.title: 💗 📄 Your resume might have the right experience, but is it showing the right inf
item.description:
💗 📄 Your resume might have the right experience, but is it showing the right information?

One mistake job seekers make is using the exact same resume for every position, even when the requirements are different.

You don't need to rewrite your entire resume for each application. A few targeted changes can make your relevant experience easier to identify.

Here's what to focus on:

1. Review the job description first.
Identify the main responsibilities, required skills and tools mentioned in the listing.

2. Adjust your professional summary.
Highlight the experience most relevant to the position instead of using the same generic introduction everywhere.

3. Reorder your bullet points.
If a position emphasizes customer support, for example, make your relevant support experience more visible rather than burying it beneath unrelated responsibilities.

4. Use specific language.
Replace vague descriptions like “helped with various tasks” with clear explanations of what you actually did.

5. Include relevant keywords naturally.
Use accurate terminology from the job description where it reflects your real experience. Don't add skills you don't have just to match the listing.

The goal isn't to make yourself look like a different candidate for every application.

It's to make it easier for hiring teams to recognize why your existing experience is relevant.

Before sending your next application, spend a few minutes reviewing your resume from the employer's perspective.
